newsitem.title: USA: Christian conservatives discover new enemy - China.
newsitem.headline: Christian conservatives discover new enemy - China.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
In a political reversal, a bevy of U.S. Christian conservative and anti-abortion groups have seized on China as a new enemy and made opposition to Beijing's trading rights their latest crusade.

Five years ago, it was mainly liberal groups who weighed into the annual battle to deny extension of most favoured nation trading status for China. Little or nothing was heard from religious conservatives on the issue.

Now, while liberals have lowered their profile, opposing MFN for China has become a rallying cry for organisations like the powerful Christian Coalition, the Family Research Council, the American Life League, Christian Solidarity International and Americans United for Life.
By opposing China, these conservative groups have opened a new front in their war against abortion -- of which, they say, the Beijing government is a leading exponent.

"China's totalitarian regime brutally oppresses its 1.2 billion people. Its policy of forced abortion destroys millions of lives and religious persecution, particularly against evangelicals and Catholics, is common," said Gary Bauer of the Family Research Council in a radio commentary broadcast last week on hundreds of Christian stations.
Perhaps the most significant development is the decision by the Christian Coalition, arguably the most powerful single bloc within the Republican Party, to oppose MFN for China.
"We have grave concerns about the mistreatment of people of faith by the Chinese government," said Heidi Stirrup, the Coalition's director of government relations.
"The Chinese government views as subversive over 100 million Buddhists, 39 million Christians and 17 million Moslems," she said.

Whereas secular groups opposing MFN for China make arguments relating to Beijing's treatment of political prisoners, its policy in Tibet and its sales of sensitive military technology to nations like Pakistan, Christian groups focus on abortion -- the one issue closest to the heart of American evangelical Protestants and Catholics.
"We are defending married couples from the inhumanity of coercive abortion policies," said John Carr of the U.S. Catholic Conference.
Analysts believe two processes may be at work in the conscious decision of the religious right to take on China.
First, religious conservatives may be searching for a new external enemy that can unite their supporters in the way that opposition to the "evil empire" of the Soviet Union did during the Cold War.
Second, organisations like the overwhelmingly white Protestant Christian Coalition are seeking to broaden their appeal by reaching out to other religious groups.
Ralph Reed, the Coalition's executive director, who will leave the organisation in September, would like to soften the group's image of zealotry.

"They are trying to broaden their moral agenda by going global," said Frank Kirkpatrick, a professor of religion at Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut. "They are looking for issues that will both resonate deeply with their own constituency while finding wider support."
Opposing persecution of Chinese Christians, most of whom are Catholics, helps build bridges with American Catholics.

"There is a great problem in the conservative movement which is there is no great external enemy after the Cold War," said Mark Rozell, a political scientist at the American University, who has studied the Christian Coalition.
"There is no glue to hold them together the way the old Soviet Union did," he said.

But China can never replace the Soviet Union as the enemy. Too much money is at stake. Many Republicans would argue that unimpeded trade with China has become crucial for U.S. exports and jobs and that cutting off MFN would hurt the United States as much as, or more than, the Chinese.
